story.text: A default password opened doors it never should have. A trusted update delivered malware. Even a security feature became a way to break in. Different stories, same problem: the things meant to protect us aren't always doing their job. Meanwhile, AI is making bug hunting faster, old flaws are still paying off, and attackers keep finding easy ways in. Some attacks take real skill. Others barely need any. This week's stories show both sides. Here's what happened. ⚡ Threat of the Week N-able 0-Days Exploited for Dropping Crypto Miners — A new set of vulnerabilities tracked as 4EverAble2Shell has come under active exploitation, with attackers exploiting it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. According to Huntback, the activity has successfully compromised 21 N-central servers across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden. Patches for the flaw are expected to be released N-able today. One Secrets Strategy for Developer and AI Agent Credentials Developer secrets and AI-agent credentials may look like separate issues, but they introduce the same access risks. Read our guide to see how a shared secrets management framework can secure developer secrets and make sure that AI agents don’t see or store raw credentials. Read Now ➝ 🔔 Top News - Compromised bee-js and Swarm Desktop Steal Swarm Wallet Keys — Threat actors compromised @ethersphere/bee-js, the JavaScript client for the Swarm storage network, with a new postinstall hook in version 13.3.0 that downloads a second stage responsible for stealing the Swarm node's wallet key and installing a backdoor. "On Linux and macOS, the backdoor is a Go remote shell," SafeDep said. "On Windows, it is a hidden ScreenConnect client that runs as SYSTEM." The same malicious code was subsequently distributed via Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 on GitHub. The activity has since been linked to a campaign called SleepyDuck (EtherDuck), which is known to spread malicious Solidity extensions through Open VSX. "The attacker controlled two Ethersphere GitHub accounts. GitHub activity logs attribute 13 pushes on November 6 to long-time maintainer nugaon," SafeDep added. "That day the attacker injected GitHub Actions workflows to steal CI credentials, and the attempts failed. Two days later, the attacker used the release bot bee-worker to publish the malicious releases. How the attacker got into either account remains unknown." - Nightmare Eclipse New SignDrop 0-Day — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges. Called SignDrop, it has been described as a Windows Common Log FileSystem (CLFS) authentication zero-day local privilege escalation flaw. "The vulnerability turns a defense into an attack surface," Cyderes said. "Microsoft added HMAC-based authentication codes to CLFS log files specifically to block the class of logic bugs caused by improper validation of CLFS data structures, which accounted for 19 of 24 CLFS CVEs over five years. SignDrop abuses the signing mechanism itself: it forces clfs.sys to create a .cnpf signature file as SYSTEM in an attacker-controlled location, producing a privileged file-creation primitive at an attacker-selected path. Because the resulting file retains attacker-accessible security attributes, the exploit reopens it and replaces the CLFS-generated content with an embedded payload DLL." Microsoft said it's investigating the reported vulnerability. In late September, the researcher also released an exploit for BigDiskBuster, a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw impacting Microsoft Defender that's similar to UnDefend and prevents the application from performing platform/signature updates. - Default Admin Password Lets Researchers Unlock and Start Cars — New research found that it's possible to take over customer accounts at two major automakers, and use them to remotely unlock and start a test car, flash headlights, and sound horns after finding an administration console on the brands' login servers still protected by its default password. Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock, an identity platform now part of Ping Identity. The carmakers remediated the flaw approximately two hours after responsible disclosure. - Google Patches Actively Exploited Chrome 0-Day — Google released updates to patch a high-severity vulnerability in Chrome has come under active exploitation in the wild. The flaw, tracked as CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: 8.8), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. The issue has been addressed in 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. Google did not disclose how the vulnerability is being exploited and in what context. - Meta Fined by Italy Over Accessing Android Users' Photos with Facebook App — The Italian Data Protection Authority (IDPA) hit Meta with one of its highest fines to date. According to the Italian data regulatory body, Meta has been fined €805 million for failing to disclose that it had access to user photos, videos, and metadata for those using the Facebook app on Android devices. Meta had access to Android users' photos and videos through a Facebook app feature that suggested content from users' personal galleries that they could post. The feature has been available since 2023. Meta has 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately. The company said it would appeal the decision. "This is a simple feature that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook," Meta told Reuters. "Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and they can change that permission at any time in their settings." ️🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. history.title: BO Team Exploits Log4Shell in VMware vCenter, Compromises Russian Firm's Code-Signing Server
history.text: An investigation into suspicious activity within a Russian software developer's network has uncovered a months-long compromise of its development infrastructure and a software code-signing server. The activity, documented by Kaspersky's ICS CERT team after it was contacted by the affected developer in June 2025, has been attributed to a threat actor named BO Team (aka Black Owl, Hoody Hyena, and Lifting Zmiy). The name of the targeted company was not disclosed, but it operates from within Russia and develops software that has a "customer base in the Russian Federation," according to Kaspersky. Over the course of several months, the intrusion resulted in the theft of confidential information and the compromise of all components of the organization's IT infrastructure, including Windows and Linux servers, workstations, hypervisors, backup servers, security solution management servers, and network equipment. Active since at least 2023, BO Team focuses on cyber espionage and hacktivism, and has a history of targeting Russian entities to steal valuable data and break into compromised infrastructure using tools like Mythic and Cobalt Strike, along with its own malware such as BrockenDoor and ZeronetKit. The group is assessed to be of Ukrainian origin. "Their primary motivation is to degrade the Russian military-industrial complex to weaken Moscow's operational capabilities on the battlefield," Orange Cyberdefense said in an analysis of the group. "They also engage in cognitive warfare aimed at humiliating Russian institutions and demonstrating their vulnerability to Ukrainian digital resistance." While BO Team is known to deploy ransomware and publicize its activities on a dedicated Telegram channel, the attack targeting the unspecified software developer did not involve any data destruction or public posts claiming responsibility for it. "Instead, the attackers worked to entrench themselves in the victim's network by setting up convenient command channels and planting backdoors to restore access in case it was lost," Kaspersky said. "The compromise of the software development (CI/CD) infrastructure and the software code-signing server indicated that the attack would likely develop into a supply chain scenario." The attack, per the Russian cybersecurity company, involved the threat actors compromising the organization's Linux terminal server by taking advantage of an exposed SSH service, and using it to conduct reconnaissance of the internal network to flag systems with accessible SMB, Kerberos, SSH, Telnet, FTP, HTTP, HTTPS, WinRM, and LDAP services. The adversary has also been found unsuccessfully attempting to access internal portals, along with websites like proxy-sale[.]com, start.duckduckgo[.]com, vcsa.vmware[.]com, and vulners[.]com, among others. Event logs show that the attackers further attempted to connect from the compromised terminal server to the virtualization system servers, including logging in to the VMware vCenter web interface. These sign-in efforts ended in failure. However, the threat actor managed to successfully target a VMware vCenter server (version 7.0.3) vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228 (aka Log4Shell and LogJam), obtain a remote command line with root privileges, connect to the hypervisor over SSH, and identify accessible hosts. This phase also involved the deployment of a backdoor on the hypervisor that was run every hour by planting a shell script in the "/etc/cron.hourly/" directory. The script carried the name "pgcache" in a likely attempt to disguise it as a legitimate PostgreSQL component. The primary responsibility of the backdoor is to download and run a secondary shell script from "lo1yaizaeghaevarooD1ahtaichootae.nofrillsdns[.]com." The shell script is designed to download and run the Global Socket (GSocket) utility, enabling the attacker to gain remote control of the compromised host. Select variants of the script have been found to point to a hostname-specific payload staged on "lo1yaizaeghaevarood1ahtaichootaz.nofrillsdns[.]com" to deliver an as-yet-undetermined next-stage payload. "The attackers used the nofrillsdns[.]com service, which allows domain names to be created for free by calling the curl utility," Kaspersky said. "By default, when the malware's command-and-control server is not operating, the attackers set the corresponding DNS record to 127.0.0.1, which is what the script checks. Activating the backdoor requires only a change to the DNS record -- the script will then download and run the malware." Some of the other post-exploitation actions undertaken by the BO Team following the backdoor deployment are listed below - - Gaining access to the corporate proxy server. - Abusing the certificate of the compromised hypervisor to connect to servers associated with a second virtualization cluster and place a similar backdoor. - Collecting information about virtual machines and firewall rules, accessing some of them via a command-line interpreter in the guest OS from the hypervisor. - Running an obfuscated bash script to decrypt and run an ELF binary designed to provide remote control over SSH. - Searching for secrets on the compromised virtual machines, allowing the attackers to breach the virtual machine of the GitLab software development platform, as well as gain access to some of the repositories containing source code and seize the server's private key. - Using the private key of the GitLab virtual machine to connect to the organization's Ansible orchestration system. - Using access to the Linux terminal server to locate credentials of several domain accounts and connect to the domain controller using the account of one of the system administrators after likely accessing the memory of virtual machines running on the compromised hypervisors. - Changing the security attributes of the user's Windows Downloads directory. - Using legitimate binaries like tasklist.exe, findstr.exe, taskmgr.exe, and ipconfig.exe to identify which security solutions were running on the system and to gather details about network interfaces. - Attempting to take a dump of the lsass.exe process using the Nanodump utility and obtain the credentials of domain administrators and other privileged users with access to the domain controller. The attackers deleted the event logs after the activity was detected and blocked by a security solution. - Using system utilities such as comsvcs.dll rather than established utilities like Mimikatz and Nanodump to create a memory dump of the lsass.exe process. - Dumping the system registry using the regedit.exe utility, and using it to decrypt the Active Directory domain database ("ntds.dit") to extract the credentials of all domain users. - Launching the OpenSSH scp.exe utility to transfer the collected information to the terminal server. - Logging in to the domain controller using the Kerberos ticket of one of the domain administrators and ultimately compromising the organization's entire Windows infrastructure by taking advantage of the fact that the same password was used for system administrator accounts in different domains. - Connecting to the terminal server over SSH using root account credentials after possibly stealing them from a system administrator's computer post obtaining domain administrator privileges. - Modifying "/usr/bin/nxnode-login" to intercept and write user credentials to a shared-memory file at "/dev/shm/pulse-shm-3088612174." - Successfully brute-forcing the password of the administrator's terminal server after about 2,500 failed attempts to place the private key of the Ansible system. - Complicating detection efforts by timestomping, obfuscation of malware code, usage of living-off-the-land (LotL) techniques, systematic deletion of event logs, and dressing up malware files as legitimate software. "We found numerous traces of BO Team connecting to various Windows servers, though the attackers only used malware in one case," Kaspersky explained. "The server which apparently held particular interest for hackers, was used to sign compiled builds of the commercial software developed by the attacked organization." "Attackers may be interested in such a server for two reasons. First, they may try to carry out a supply chain attack by injecting malicious code into a product build right before it is signed. Second, the attackers may try to steal the organization's digital signature to use later to sign malware." It's suspected that the attackers likely attempted to execute a malicious WMI script and install a backdoor similar to the Linux variant in the temporary files directory. But after the incident was detected and countermeasures were enacted, the attackers, after having lost access to the compromised infrastructure, orchestrated a phishing campaign towards the end of July in an attempt to collect employee credentials. The phishing email contained the "Account disconnected from the mail server" subject line and sought to trick the recipient into clicking on a link to change their password. What's more, the email managed to bypass SPF and DKIM checks, indicating the attackers had in their possession a private key that was obtained after gaining control of the organization's mail server. The phishing attack was detected and prevented. "The attackers used a service that automatically generates phishing pages," Kaspersky said. "The service loads the content of a targeted organization's official website and displays a password entry form on top of the official site's layout. After entering the password, the user sees an error message. However, the information is actually sent to the attacker." "We repeatedly noted that the attackers tried not to use malware and hacking utilities in order to evade detection," Kaspersky said. "Instead, they actively used system tools such as RDP, SSH, and SCP, as well as system utilities to steal user credentials. This enabled them to develop the attack using legitimate accounts, which also matches the BO Team prof
history.summary: BO Team exploited CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) to compromise a VMware vCenter server version 7.0.3, gaining root-level remote command access. The threat actor deployed a persistent backdoor via a cron.hourly shell script named "pgcache" that downloaded and executed a secondary script from a nofrillsdns[.]com domain to enable remote control via the GSocket utility. After months of network-wide intrusion and attempted supply chain compromise of the code-signing server, rapid response measures cut off attacker access before a malicious code injection could be deployed.

history.title: Barracuda links cloud breach to ARTEX AI-powered cyberattack
history.text: Hackers who breached the cloud environment of network and email security company Barracuda earlier this month used a stolen cloud access key and the ARTEX AI penetration testing framework. The company says the attacker accessed approximately 10 of its cloud accounts over a 44-hour period between November 1 and 2. The attacker's presence was discovered on November 4, and Barracuda's investigation determined that the open-source AI pentesting framework ARTEX was used for this "machine-speed intrusion." The company explains that the attacker leveraged a cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor for the duration of a previous project. "We did not retire the key when the vendor — a company working in AI — finished that work. That is on us," Barracuda says. The security company believes the attacker stole the key from the unnamed third-party AI vendor in October. It confirmed that the key was stored in a configuration file in the vendor's GitHub repository. The attacker used credentials they found in one system to move through Barracuda’s data analytics environment, source-code repositories, and Kubernetes clusters. Based on the attacker's commands targeting cryptocurrency-related secrets, including private keys, Ethereum keystore files, and seed phrases, Barracuda believes the attack was financially motivated. However, the company does not rule out that this activity might have been a diversion from the attacker’s true motive. The threat actor attempted to establish persistence by deploying a container that mounted the host’s file system, including credentials stored on it. A separate attempt to create a new cloud administrator identity was blocked. Barracuda says the attack used machine-style labels, certain probing methods, and built-in hunting routines that matched what is found in ARTEX. The firm noted that the attack was very similar to a recent incident at cloud hosting provider Railway, which also involved credential chaining and the apparent use of ARTEX. According to the cybersecurity company, the attacker reached a system that stores customer integration credentials for Barracuda XDR; however, it found no evidence that those were accessed or stolen. Because of the uncertainty surrounding this scenario, Barracuda asked potentially affected Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint customers to revoke and recreate their integration credentials. history.title: Microsoft says months-old bug caused global Microsoft 365 outage
history.text: Microsoft says a software bug introduced in July caused last week's worldwide Microsoft 365 outage, triggering a cascading failure that left more than 80% of its networking gateway servers unresponsive. The nearly 24-hour outage on November 12 disrupted Microsoft 365 services worldwide, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot, leaving users unable to access their email and causing significant delays in message delivery. In a preliminary post-incident report shared in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center, the company said the outage was caused by three problems: a previously undetected software bug, increased traffic after a Microsoft Teams failover, and reduced server capacity. The incident began at 11:20 AM ET on Thursday, November 12, and continued until 11:10 AM ET the following day, when Microsoft confirmed that services were full restored. According to Microsoft, the software bug was introduced in July through an update developed for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. While the update had been deployed for more than three months without issues, it contained a bug that could overwhelm servers under certain traffic conditions, causing them to stop responding. Microsoft says its tests of the update did not detect the bug as it used less powerful testing hardware than the production servers. "Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the traffic mix and SKUs used in our labs," Microsoft explained in its preliminary report. "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The bug was eventually triggered after Microsoft Teams automatically switched to the networking infrastructure used by Exchange Online approximately 15 hours before the outage, increasing traffic on those servers. Microsoft Teams also experienced a separate outage earlier that day, but it is unclear whether the two incidents are related. To make matters worse, Microsoft says nearly 14% of the gateway's server capacity was already offline due to an unrelated issue. While the infrastructure had sufficient capacity to handle the reduction, the combination of increased traffic and reduced capacity triggered the software bug. As servers stopped responding, Microsoft's systems redirected users to other available servers, which also became overwhelmed by the additional traffic and failed as well. "In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive," explained Microsoft. Microsoft says safeguards designed to prevent problems from spreading between regions also failed to contain the cascading outages, allowing the disruption to spread worldwide. While other Microsoft 365 services, like Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint, could switch to alternative infrastructure and recover earlier, Exchange Online could not make the same switch, leaving users unable to access their mailboxes. Microsoft says recovery was difficult because restarting affected servers caused them to be quickly overwhelmed again by backed-up traffic. After identifying the bug, Microsoft engineers developed a fix and deployed it across affected servers, allowing services to stabilize throughout Friday. Microsoft confirmed that active customer impact had ended by 11:10 AM ET on November 13. The company says it has since increased capacity, improved monitoring, and added safeguards to prevent traffic redirection from triggering similar cascading failures. In a separate statement on X, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, apologized for the disruption. "We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations," Lamanna said. Microsoft says its investigation is continuing, with a final post-incident report expected later this week. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. More than 80% of servers became unresponsive, and Microsoft later deployed a fix that stabilized services after identifying the latent defect.

history.title: Cursor Supply Chain Attack Started at Fireworks AI
history.text: Credentials compromised in the hack of AI inference platform Fireworks AI allowed attackers to steal more secrets and push malicious Claude Code extension copies, Cursor says. The supply chain attack was discovered on October 29 and resulted in threat actors making two modified versions of the anthropic.claude-code extension (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) available through the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace for roughly 11 hours. Anthropic was never hacked, and all the malicious activity occurred in Cursor’s environment, the company explains. Instead, Cursor was hit after Fireworks was hacked twice in October. First, internal Fireworks credentials were used to access Fireworks stored secrets and account and billing information. Then, a third-party cloud provider was compromised, Fireworks development machines were reached, and customer data was stolen. A Cursor access key issued to Fireworks was compromised in one of these incidents and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket, including unredacted credentials that opened the door to SaaS tools used by Cursor. “From these tools they accessed select archived non-production Cursor source code repositories (some containing business contact information), limited customer support data and email conversations, product usage metrics and contact details, summaries of some coding agent conversations, and some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team,” Cursor explains. While Cursor blocked the attacker’s access immediately after discovering the unauthorized activity, the attacker used secrets exfiltrated from the company’s internal systems to place “malicious, unauthorized copies of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace.” The malware was never present in the Open VSX marketplace source, but was served to the users who requested the cached versions of the extension. According to Cursor, at most 5,000 users were affected. “If customers installed or updated to the tampered version Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace during the exposure window, we ask customers to follow the steps in our security notice. Uninstalling the extension alone may not be enough,” Cursor notes. The company considers the incident contained, as it has not seen attacker activity in its environment since November 1. Notion and Uber also disclosed data breaches stemming from the Fireworks compromise. history.summary: Cursor disclosed a supply chain attack traced to compromises at Fireworks AI, where stolen credentials allowed threat actors to publish two malicious versions (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) of the anthropic.claude-code extension through the Cursor VS Code Marketplace for about 11 hours, affecting up to 5,000 users; the malware was served via cache and was never in the Open VSX source, and Anthropic's systems were not breached. The incident was discovered on October 29, Cursor blocked access the same day, and the company considers the event contained with no observed attacker activity since November 1, recommending affected users follow its security notice as uninstalling alone may not suffice. Fix: Customers who installed or updated to the tampered extension versions 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 during the exposure window should follow Cursor's security notice steps for remediation.

history.title: Fandango says hackers stole payment card details from checkout pages
history.text: Ticket seller Fandango Media is notifying customers about a data breach that exposed payment card details entered on its checkout pages. The company says the details were exposed between October 8 and 11, and it impacts customers who made purchases through its official website. Card skimmer code injected into Fandango’s checkout page intercepted payment card details entered when placing orders, sending the data to hackers. Fandango Media is a major U.S. online movie ticketing platform. It sells tickets through its website and app for 31,000 U.S. cinema screens, including at AMC, Regal, and Cinemark. The company also operates the popular movie review website Rotten Tomatoes. “Our investigation identified evidence that an unauthorized party could access payment card information associated with certain transactions on our checkout page from October 8-11, 2026,” reads the notification to customers. “Fandango determined on October 30, 2026 that your information may have been impacted in this incident.” The company says the following data types may have been exposed: - Payment card number - CVV (verification code) - Expiration date - Billing ZIP (postal code) - Email address Fandango says the incident did not expose names, government-issued identity information, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or any other account information. However, the information compromised in the incident could be used for unauthorized purchases on online stores. To reduce the risk to affected customers, Fandango is offering two years of free IDX credit and dark web monitoring, as well as identity theft recovery services, with an enrollment deadline of February 13, 2027. Fandango says it has now fixed the issue on its checkout page, investigated with outside cybersecurity specialists, and is currently unaware of any cases of fraud leveraging the stolen data. The company has not shared the number of affected customers. BleepingComputer has contacted Fandango to learn more, and we will update this post with their response once received. Users who bought movie tickets from Fandango during the exposure window should monitor their statements and account activity closely, and report any unauthorized purchases to their card issuer. One way to protect payment card details is to use one-time virtual cards when making online purchases. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. history.title: Barracuda Hacked Amid Surge in Artex-Powered Cyberattacks
history.text: The Artex agentic AI penetration testing framework has become a common tool in Chinese threat actors’ arsenal, and Barracuda is one of its victims. Published on GitHub in July 2026, Artex relies on a planner to formulate an objective and create tasks based on it, and on agents to perform those tasks, while the platform itself records the progress, findings, and assets. It reportedly used DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the initial model, but can use other LLMs as well, and GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6 were observed in certain instances. Overall, however, its users mainly rely on Chinese models, which are more permissive compared to US-made ones. Artex was designed for security testing, but threat actors have been using it as part of in-the-wild intrusions since at least August, and its occurrence in real-world attacks has increased significantly during the past several weeks. “The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale,” the FBI warns in a new alert (PDF). Mentioning the framework’s use in attacks on South Korean financial firms and ConnectWise, the FBI warns of the risks Artex poses: faster attacks through automation, exploitation of neglected peripheral devices, and the ability to find and exploit supply chain attack vectors. The framework’s developer removed their GitHub repository in October, but Artex continues to proliferate through other channels. In early November, Censys was seeing roughly 1,500 hosts running exposed Artex consoles. In October, Artex was used by Chinese espionage group Vapor Panda in a campaign targeting over 200 organizations in 14 countries, including “foreign ministries, a European presidency, and US pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, and nuclear organizations,” SentinelOne reports. Storm-0940 is another Chinese state-sponsored group using Artex, but evidence shows that financially motivated threat actors such as Storm-3358 have also adopted the framework, Cisco’s Talos notes. Post-exploitation, the threat actors were seen abusing compromised credentials and keys, escalating privileges, deploying persistence, moving laterally, and stealing credentials and data. “Observed impacts range from access to cloud secrets and mailbox data to the use of compromised applications to reach connected environments,” Talos says. Amazon describes similar observations, noting that one of the most prominent Artex campaigns was focused on large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, while another targeted cryptocurrency exchanges. Barracuda, which fell victim to an Artex-powered intrusion, published similar findings: hackers used an exposed valid cloud access key to map its reach, then reused discovered secrets to access more systems and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets. “In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours. The work was methodical and tireless. The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match Artex,” Barracuda explains. The attack unfolded between November 1 and November 2, targeted sensitive material across secret stores, configurations, Kubernetes service accounts, and server metadata services, and left a backdoor behind in a Kubernetes cluster. On some servers, the attackers gained shell access and used it to search for Ethereum keystore files, seed phrase files, extended private keys, and other wallet-related information. The attack, Barracuda says, was similar to the October intrusion at cloud application hosting platform Railway. Furthermore, it fits the previously reported wave of intrusions at dozens of AI developer platforms. Barracuda has not attributed the attack, noting that Artex is used by many groups. Amazon’s analysis of two Artex-powered campaigns revealed that the attackers relied on long-known techniques, but operated at far greater speeds courtesy of AI. “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software. Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense,” Amazon says. “The reported Artex activity shows that autonomous attackers don’t need a zero-day. They can find exposed services, exploit authorization gaps, and keep adapting while defenders are still triaging alerts and approving a response. When every defensive action has to wait for a person, the attacker controls the pace. Defenders need to move from identifying exposure to verified protection at machine speed,” Miggo Security co-founder and CEO Daniel Shechter said. Related: Is AI Making Us Worse at Cybersecurity? Related: OpenAI Unveils Daybreak Red Team, Defense Factory Security Tools Related: Notion Customer Data Compromised in Fireworks AI Hack Related: Google Widens Gemini 4 Carbon Access After AI Agents Verify Signal Code
history.summary: Barracuda fell victim to an Artex-powered intrusion where attackers used an exposed cloud access key to map systems, reuse secrets, and exfiltrate credentials across about 10 accounts in roughly 44 hours, targeting secret stores, Kubernetes service accounts, and server metadata services while leaving a backdoor in a Kubernetes cluster. The Artex agentic AI framework, originally designed for security testing, has been adopted by Chinese state-sponsored and financially motivated threat actors to automate multi-target operations, enabling faster attacks through exploitation of neglected devices, default or hardcoded credentials, unauthenticated interfaces, and unpatched software.

history.title: 7 Tips For Complying with CJIS Password and MFA Requirements
history.text: Compromised passwords and gaps in multi-factor authentication (MFA) remain common ways attackers gain access to sensitive systems. For law enforcement agencies handling criminal justice information (CJI), protecting against these threats is also a matter of CJIS compliance. The FBI's latest CJIS Security Policy sets clear requirements for password management and MFA. these are Priority 1 (P1) controls, so must be implemented immediately to comply. But this can be challenging, particularly across the complex IT environments that are common in law enforcement. This guide contains practical tips to help agencies meet the latest requirements, strengthen their defenses against credential-based attacks, and make ongoing compliance easier to manage. 1. Enforce Stronger Minimum Password Lengths CJIS requires user-selected passwords to be at least eight characters long, or six characters if generated by a credential service provider or verifier using an approved random number generator. However, we recommend going beyond these minimums and encouraging passphrases of at least 15 characters. Longer passwords are generally harder to crack, and passphrases can be easier to remember than shorter passwords with complex combinations of symbols and numbers. CJIS doesn't require traditional complexity rules, so focus on length and strength rather than arbitrary character requirements. 2. Block Weak and Compromised Passwords Agencies must maintain a list of commonly used, predictable, and compromised passwords. This should include passwords exposed in previous breaches, dictionary words, sequential characters, and context-specific terms such as usernames or agency names. CJIS requires agencies to update this list at least quarterly, and whenever organizational passwords are suspected of being compromised. Solutions like Specops Password Policy with Breached Password Protection can simplify this process with CJIS-aligned password policy templates. You can create an unlimited custom dictionary of blocked words unique to your agency, with granular controls for blocking weak constructions. Importantly, the Breached Password Protection feature delivers continuous screening against a growing database of more than six billion compromised passwords. Secure your Active Directory passwords with Specops Password Policy Verizon’s Data Breach Investigation Report found stolen credentials are involved in 44.7% of breaches. Effortlessly secure Active Directory with compliant password policies, blocking 4+ billion compromised passwords, boosting security, and slashing support hassles! 3. Reset Passwords Quickly and Give Users Clear Feedback Agencies must force a password change whenever there's evidence that a credential has been compromised. Don't rely solely on scheduled password changes to address exposed credentials. You must also check existing passwords against the breach list at least quarterly. More regular checks can help identify compromised credentials earlier, giving IT teams an opportunity to respond before attackers exploit them. CJIS also requires users to select a new password immediately whenever compromise is suspected. When a user does need to create or reset a password, rather than displaying a generic error message, provide clear, real-time feedback that helps users understand what makes a password weak and how to improve it. Specops Password Policy delivers that support, making it easier to create strong, memorable passwords while reducing frustration and unnecessary help desk requests. 4. Protect Passwords in Transit and At Rest Password security doesn't end with enforcing strong credentials. CJIS also requires passwords to be transmitted over encrypted, authenticated channels to prevent interception and man-in-the-middle attacks. When stored, passwords must be salted and hashed using a suitable one-way key derivation function, making them more resistant to offline cracking if an authentication database is compromised. Agencies should review how their applications and authentication systems handle credentials to ensure these protections are in place. 5. Require MFA For All Privileged and Non-Privileged Accounts CJIS requires MFA for both privileged and non-privileged organizational accounts. Don't focus solely on administrator accounts. Standard user accounts can also give attackers access to sensitive data or provide a foothold for further attacks. Review your accounts and access policies to identify where MFA is missing, including accounts belonging to employees and contractors. 6. Extend MFA Across All Relevant Access Methods CJIS requires MFA for local, network, and remote access. Agencies should review authentication across their environment, ensuring that all systems that touch CJI are adequately protected. Solutions such as Specops Secure Access helps agencies extend MFA to Windows logons, RDP, and VPN connections, with single sign-on (SSO) support for compatible SaaS applications through OIDC and SAML. 7. Make Sure Your MFA Methods Meet CJIS Requirements CJIS specifies Authenticator Assurance Level 2 (AAL2), which requires two different authentication factors. This is a combination of something you know (like a password), something you have (like a smart card), or something you are (like a fingerprint). Review your authentication methods to ensure they meet these requirements. Where possible, consider phishing-resistant MFA methods to provide stronger protection against credential phishing and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Keep Your Authentication Controls Effective CJIS compliance doesn't end once you've implemented strong password policies and MFA. Regularly reviewing your authentication controls, checking for compromised credentials, and auditing Active Directory can help you identify security gaps before attackers exploit them. As a starting point, Specops Password Auditor performs a free, read-only AD audit that checks for weak or compromised passwords and inactive privileged administrator accounts. You’ll get the results in an easy-to understand interactive report that highlights your current exposure. By combining strong authentication controls with regular security assessments, agencies can reduce credential-related risks and make ongoing CJIS compliance easier to manage. If you’re interested in seeing how Specops solutions can help your agency comply with CJIS standards, book a demo today. Sponsored and written by Specops Software.

Agencies must maintain and quarterly update a list of commonly used, compromised, and predictable passwords, and force immediate password changes when credentials are suspected of being exposed. CJIS mandates multi-factor authentication at Authenticator Assurance Level 2 for all privileged and non-privileged accounts across local, network, and remote access, requiring two different authentication factors.

history.title: Retadup Worm Resurfaces 7 Years After Takedown to Spread CoffeeLoader Malware
history.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader, a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines. "On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky said in an analysis published today. "The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer." CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode. The malware is assessed to share source code similarities with another loader family tracked as SmokeLoader. Malware packed with Armory uses file names like "ArmouryAIOSDK.dll" and "ArmouryA.dll," with the packer hijacking some of the original Armoury Crate functionality with self-decrypting shellcode. Notably, the shellcode extracts code that executes a decryption routine on a system's GPU by making use of the OpenCL library. The end goal is to install CoffeeLoader, establish persistence, and execute it by injecting it into a newly created "dllhost.exe" process. The latest version of the packer continues to use the GPU, but replaces OpenCL with the OpenGL library. In addition, the new version of the packer delivers intermediate shellcode instead of a DLL. This shellcode serves as a downloader responsible for fetching the main CoffeeLoader malware. "To establish persistence, the Trojan copies '7z.dll' to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%," Kaspersky said. "The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information." "To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager." Once persistence is successful, the malware launches one of the legitimate processes (e.g., "dllhost.exe," "WerFault.exe," "svchost.exe," "OpenWith.exe," or "AtBroker.exe") and then injects itself into it, after which the malware shellcode is downloaded from a hard-coded command-and-control (C2) server. The shellcode then decrypts and runs the CoffeeLoader payload. It supports the same three commands to run the next-stage malware from the C2 server - - Injecting it into a process - Saving it to disk as an executable and then running it - Saving it as a DLL and then running it via "rundll32.exe" As for how CoffeeLoader is distributed, it takes place via Retadup, a Windows computer worm that was disrupted by French law enforcement authorities in August 2019. The malware, which spreads via infected USB drives, has been used to drop additional payloads like cryptocurrency miners, the Stop ransomware, and the Arkei password stealer. "Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware," Kaspersky said. "At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader." It remains unclear whether the worm's author or some other threat actor was instrumental in bringing the C2 servers back online. Kaspersky said it blocked around 15,000 systems from being infected with the resurrected version of the worm, most of them located in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.
history.summary: A new variant of CoffeeLoader malware has been discovered using a patched 7-Zip library (7z.dll) with Armoury packer shellcode to resist analysis and gain persistence on infected systems. The malware is distributed through the resurrected Retadup worm, whose former command-and-control domains were re-registered around two years ago and now serve CoffeeLoader instead of the original SmokeLoader. Kaspersky reported blocking approximately 15,000 infection attempts worldwide, with the majority of targets located in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

history.title: Uber Data Breach Impacts 150,000 People
history.text: Uber is notifying roughly 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in a data breach involving a third-party services provider. The company learned of the incident on October 9 and immediately severed its data connections with the provider and launched an investigation. On October 13, the investigation determined that the hackers used compromised service provider credentials on October 7 to access data Uber had shared with the provider. According to Uber, the hackers accessed images of driver’s licenses and personal information such as names, addresses, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers, and government-issued ID numbers. The company says that the data was stored in an environment created and managed by Uber’s Cloud Security team. While alerts were enabled, none were triggered because the threat actor used valid credentials. “The service provider’s compromised credentials did not provide access to other Uber systems. The investigation remains ongoing,” the company said. Uber has filed data breach notifications with multiple US states, including California, Iowa, Massachusetts, South Carolina, Texas, and Vermont, and reportedly notified the Texas Attorney General’s Office that a total of 149,346 people were affected. Uber is providing the potentially affected individuals with free credit monitoring and fraud assistance services. Uber did not identify the service provider in its breach notifications, but a company spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that the incident involved Fireworks AI, a cloud platform for running and fine-tuning open source AI models. Fireworks initially said it had found no evidence that customer personal information, models or datasets had been accessed. However, in a November 9 update, the company acknowledged that the breach also affected account and billing information, as well as some customer datasets and incomplete models. SecurityWeek has emailed Uber for additional information on the data breach and will update this article if the company responds. history.title: ConnectWise Warns ScreenConnect Attacks Continue as SCKit Targets Unpatched Systems
history.text: ConnectWise on Monday said it completed its investigation into unauthorized access targeting partner ScreenConnect environments, and recommended customers to ensure that the technician client is running version 26.6.5 or later. The company said additional activity targeting on-premises environments continues to be reported where the identified third-party extensions remain enabled and ScreenConnect has not been updated to the latest version. "On-premises partners must immediately disable the identified extensions and update ScreenConnect to the latest supported version," the company said. It's worth noting that version 26.6.5 addresses a critical-severity flaw in ScreenConnect client tracked as CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9) that could allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation in certain circumstances. As highlighted by Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber last week, unknown threat actors are suspected to be exploiting an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 to execute unauthorized commands while bypassing ScreenConnect's regular authentication controls. The attacks have been found to deploy a multi-component toolkit dubbed SCKit that's capable of spreading from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromising additional managed networks by means of a C# module called RelayTrap ("RelayTrap.cs"). Specifically, the malware employs a worm-like technique that exploits CVE-2026-84869 to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device to investigate a problem. There is no evidence this worm-like behavior has succeeded in the latest campaign. Huntress has since said it detected another spike in SCKit-related activity on November 13, 2026, impacting 205 hosts across 41 organizations. "Across the incidents, we saw the new ScreenConnect client being hosted at 185.241.211[.]197, which is associated with 1337 Services GmbH, a bulletproof hosting provider known for previously hosting malicious traffic," the company said. "In one of the incidents, we saw a rogue ScreenConnect client establish persistence via a service called Windows Update Agent, posing as a legitimate system component. The service executable (UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe) was placed in C:\ProgramData\Windows Update Agent (de362a425905bcc4)\ and configured to run under the LocalSystem account." In response to the incident, ConnectWise has taken the step of disabling five third-party extensions, including Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link, across 400 partner environments. That said, the presence of these extensions alone does not imply those environments were impacted. The company is also urging partners not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance. "Disabling extensions and updating software do not remove unauthorized access or persistence already established on affected devices," it added.
history.summary: ConnectWise confirmed ongoing attacks targeting unpatched ScreenConnect environments, exploiting CVE-2026-84869 to allow unauthorized file transfer and execution. The company recommends updating to version 26.6.5 or later and immediately disabling five identified third-party extensions across affected partner environments. Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber reported threat actors exploiting RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 to bypass authentication and deploy the SCKit toolkit, which spreads worm-like attacks to technician workstations.

history.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
history.text: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. - CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. history.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-115731, a Perforce Puppet Enterprise deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog based on evidence of active exploitation. The addition falls under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, which requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities on publicly exposed assets that grant total control post-exploitation. CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and will continue adding vulnerabilities that meet the catalog's criteria.
